newsitem.title: USA: Donnelley has "cordial" meeting with Jackson.
newsitem.headline: Donnelley has "cordial" meeting with Jackson.

text.p: R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co., which was hit with a $500 million racial discrimination suit last week, held "cordial" talks with Rev. Jesse Jackson Monday, but the civil rights leader later said he might organize demonstrations against the printing giant.

Jonathan Ward, president of R.R. Donnelley's commercial printing sector, described the 45-minute session as "cordial and productive" and said he and others would meet again next Monday with Jackson and colleagues from the Rainbow PUSH Action Network.
"There were no threats, veiled or otherwise, from Rev. Jackson," Ward said in an interview.

"We will look to them to answer our questions, then enter negotiations. If that breaks down then you have demonstrations," Jackson said later, noting that the printer's clients might be sensitive to its employment policies.

"They were not willing to offer an explanation at this point because of the lawsuits," Jackson told reporters outside Donnelley's downtown headquarters where pickets from PUSH marched for several hours.
Jackson called Donnelley's pattern of discrimination against black workers worse than a recently settled case involving black executives at Texaco Inc.
"The charges against them are more egregious than Texaco," Jackson said. "A group of black and white workers were downsized and systematically forced into retirement."
Last month, Texaco paid $176 million to settle a 1994 discrimination suit brought by a group of black plaintiffs.

Jackson and other black leaders threatened a nationwide boycott against Texaco, but he was not specific about his plans for Donnelley. The company is the world's largest commercial printer and publishes phone books, magazines, newspaper inserts, government documents and other material.
Jackson said he sought data on the location and makeup of the printing company's domestic workforce and "other research."

"To the best of our ability we said we would provide the information as long as it did not involve any litigation," Ward said. "We will do it in a timely way, whether before or at the meeting (next week)."
Donnelley employs about 40,000 people worldwide, including 36,000 workers domestically. Ward said 13 percent of the company's workforce are members of minority groups and 7 percent are black.

The class-action lawsuit filed Nov. 25 in federal court in Chicago alleged the company discriminated against black employees when arranging transfers to other jobs related to a 1994 plant closing. The suit contended that only seven of the plant's 575 black workers were eventually transferred to other locations, compared to 140 out of 400 white workers.

Jackson noted that the lawsuit against Donnelley charged the company classified black workers with up to 30 years experience as "temporary" employees. The suit said 94 percent of its temporary Chicago workers were black.
Ward reiterated the company's policy of "zero tolerance of discrimination. I've been with this company for 19 years, and our practices line up very soundly behind that."
"We don't find any basis for the claim," he added.
